title: Taking Part in Your Community
tagline: Speak up, bring evidence, and help decisions get made.
description: Decisions about your area are made in meetings you can take part in. Learn how to prepare, how to present a problem with evidence, and how to engage respectfully with officials and councillors.
outcomes: Know where community decisions are made
Prepare before a meeting or consultation
Present a problem clearly, with evidence
Report a community problem and follow it up

lessons.title: Where decisions are made
lessons.body:
Many decisions about your area are made in meetings that are open to residents.

## Places to take part
Ward development meetings, council meetings and public consultations are where plans and budgets are discussed. Community radio and notice boards often share when these happen.

## Why it matters
When residents take part, decisions reflect real needs. Showing up and speaking is one of the simplest ways to shape your community.
key_points: Ward meetings and consultations are open to residents
Plans and budgets are discussed there
Radio and notice boards share the dates
Taking part helps decisions reflect real needs
lessons.try_it: Find out when the next community or ward meeting in your area is.

lessons.title: Speak up with evidence
lessons.body:
A point lands better when it is clear and backed by facts.

## Prepare first
Decide the one thing you want to say. Write it in a sentence or two. Bring evidence: a photo, a date, a number of people affected, or a simple example.

## Be constructive
Speak calmly and respectfully, even when you disagree. Offer a suggestion, not only a complaint. Thank people for listening.
key_points: Decide the one point you want to make
Bring simple evidence: a photo, a date, a number
Offer a suggestion, not only a complaint
lessons.try_it: Pick one issue and write the single sentence you would say about it.

lessons.title: Reporting a community problem
lessons.body:
Reporting a problem well makes it more likely to be fixed.

## A real situation
A borehole in your area has been broken for weeks. Who do you tell? Start with your ward councillor or the responsible office. Explain clearly: where it is, how long it has been broken, and how many people it affects.

## Follow it up
Ask what will happen next and when. Keep a note of who you spoke to. If nothing changes, follow up politely and, if needed, raise it at a community meeting.
key_points: Report to your councillor or the responsible office
Say where, how long, and how many are affected
Ask what happens next and when
Follow up and raise it at a meeting if needed
lessons.try_it: Think of one real problem near you. Write who you would tell and what you would say.

quiz.question: Where are many decisions about your area discussed?
quiz.explanation: Ward meetings, council meetings and public consultations are open to residents.

quiz.question: What makes a point land well at a meeting?
quiz.explanation: A clear point backed by simple evidence, offered respectfully, lands best.
